<explanation>
Below is a step-by-step guide, tailored to the V2Ray-core project, on how to produce a detailed system-design diagram that accurately reflects its architecture.

1. Identify the project type and purpose
   • V2Ray-core is a modular, Go-based network proxy engine.  
   • It handles inbound and outbound connections, routing, DNS resolution, transport protocols, statistics and logging.  
   • It exposes a CLI/API entry point and a gRPC control plane, and is built via Bazel and Go modules.

2. Analyze the file structure
   Top-level directories:
   – app: “application layer” that initializes modules, wiring CLI or service commands.  
   – proxy: implementations of inbound/outbound protocols (vmess, shadowsocks, socks, HTTP, MTProto, Trojan, etc.).  
   – transport: network transport layers (TCP, UDP, KCP, QUIC, WebSocket, domain sockets, TLS/XTLS, pipe).  
   – common: shared utilities (buffer, crypto, mux, session, protocol definitions, signal, task, etc.).  
   – infra: build & config infrastructure (Bazel BUILD files, config loaders, control API, gRPC stub generation).  
   – main: actual binaries and distributors (confloader, distro targets, JSON exporters).  
   – release, testing, Dockerfile, workflows: packaging, CI/CD, tests.

3. Extract additional insights from README
   • Core functionality: secure network proxying and routing.  
   • Third-party dependencies: gorilla/websocket, gRPC (for control plane), miekg/dns (test), h12w/socks (test).

4. How to create the system-design diagram

   a. Identify main components
      1. Control Plane & CLI Layer  
         – main binaries (main/, app/commander, infra/control)  
         – gRPC API servers and protobuf definitions  
      2. Configuration Loader  
         – infra/conf, main/confloader  
         – config.proto .pb.go files  
      3. Core Engine  
         – app dispatcher (app/dispatcher)  
         – router & policy manager (app/router, app/policy)  
         – DNS resolver (app/dns)  
         – stats & logging (app/stats, app/log)  
      4. Protocol Proxy Modules  
         – proxy/* (vmess, vless, shadowsocks, socks, trojan, http, dokodemo, freedom, blackhole, mtproto)  
      5. Transport Layer  
         – transport/internet (TCP, UDP, KCP, QUIC, WebSocket, Domain Sockets, TLS/XTLS)  
         – transport/pipe  
      6. Common Utilities  
         – common/* (buffer, crypto, mux, protocol, session, signal, task, retry, uuid)  
      7. External Networks & Services  
         – Upstream servers (remote proxies, origin servers)  
         – DNS servers  
         – Control-plane clients (UI, management tools)

   b. Show relationships and data flows
      1. CLI/Control Plane → Configuration Loader → Core Engine  
      2. Core Engine inbound listener → Dispatcher → Router/Policy → Outbound proxy module  
      3. DNS module invoked by Router or proxies → External DNS servers → DNS cache  
      4. Transport layer sits beneath proxies to perform actual network I/O  
      5. Stats & Logging subscribe to events from Core Engine and Protocol modules  
      6. Control Plane gRPC → live config updates → Core Engine components  

   c. Highlight architectural patterns & design principles
      • Plugin-style modules: each proxy protocol implements a common inbound/outbound interface.  
      • Separation of concerns: config parsing, business logic (routing/dispatch), transport I/O, utilities.  
      • Event-based stats/logging and pub/sub (common/signal/pubsub).  
      • Dependency injection via context and config structs.  
      • Protobuf/gRPC for code generation and control APIs.

   d. Relevant technologies
      • Go modules, Bazel (infra/bazel)  
      • Protobuf definitions (.proto) across app, infra, proxy, router, stats  
      • gRPC (command_grpc.pb.go) for control services  
      • gorilla/websocket for WebSocket transport  

5. Tailoring the diagram to this full-stack network proxy
   • Emphasize clear separation:  
     – Top: CLI/Control-plane  
     – Middle: Core Engine & Protocol proxies  
     – Bottom: Transport layer & external network  
   • Show plugin points: each proxy protocol as a swappable block  
   • Illustrate data path: ingress → dispatch → egress  

6. Diagramming guidelines
   • Use clear, descriptive labels for each component (e.g., “Inbound: VMess”, “Router: GeoIP” “Transport: KCP”)  
   • Draw directional arrows for data flow and dependencies (e.g., inbound → dispatcher → outbound)  
   • Color-code by layer:  
     – Blue: Control/CLI  
     – Green: Core Engine & Features  
     – Orange: Protocol modules (proxy/*)  
     – Red: Transport modules (transport/*)  
     – Grey: Common utilities  
   • Use distinct shapes (e.g., cylinders for external systems like DNS, rectangles for modules, parallelograms for configuration files)

7. Final tips
   • Capture every top-level package as a component or subcomponent in your diagram.  
   • Annotate arrows with method calls or interfaces (e.g., Dispatch(), Route(), Dial()).  
   • Include a legend for colors and shapes.  
   • Be as granular as practical—this is a library/executable with dozens of modules, so grouping related subpackages under a single box (e.g., “Proxy Modules”) is acceptable to avoid clutter.  
   • Ensure the diagram shows both control-plane and data-plane paths.

By following these steps and structuring your diagram around the layers and modules detailed above, you will produce a comprehensive, accurate architecture overview of V2Ray-core.  
</explanation>
